speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Good afternoon and welcome to the Skyworks Solutions second quarter fiscal year 2023 earnings call. This call is being recorded. At this time, I will turn the call over to Mitch Hayes, investor relations for Skyworks. Mr. Hayes, please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk07
speakers.text: Thank you, Joelle. Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Skyworks second fiscal quarter 2023 conference call. With me today are Liam Griffin, our chairman, chief executive officer and president, and Chris Senesal, our Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that our discussion will include statements relating to future results and expectations that are or may be considered forward-looking statements. Please refer to our earnings press release and recent SEC filings, including our annual report on Form 10-K, for information on certain risks that could cause actual outcomes to differ materially and adversely from any forward-looking statements made today. The results and guidance we will discuss include non-GAAP financial measures consistent with our past practice. Please refer to our press release within the investor relations section of our company website for complete reconciliation to GAAP. With that, I'll turn the call to Liam.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Thanks, Mitch, and welcome, everyone. The Skyworks team executed well in a challenging market environment, delivering second quarter revenue above consensus estimates with solid profitability and strong cash flow generation. Looking at Q2 in more detail, we delivered revenue of $1,153,000,000. We drove gross margin of 50% and operating margin of 33.5%. We posted earnings per share of $2.02 and we generated $412,000,000 of operating cash flow. In addition to the financial results, we expanded our design wind pipeline reflecting our success in diversifying our customer base and product portfolio. Across mobile and IoT, we delivered Sky5 platforms for Samsung's newly released smartphones. We launched Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 gateways for CommScope and Asus. And we secured 5G content with a mobile computing leader. Across infrastructure and industrial, we enable small cell deployments with a Japanese telecommunications company. We provided enhanced power over ethernet functionality to Cisco for their enterprise networks. We shipped programmable timing solutions to the top US satellite provider and leveraged our expanding industrial product suite with a leader in smart meter technology. In automotive, we continue to post year-over-year revenue growth while capturing EV onboard charging content with a top European supplier and ramping digital radio products with a leading Korean OEM. These engagements highlight the increasingly diverse and expansive nature of our business, supporting the broadest array of customers and applications in our history. Several key market trends underscore the growth potential of advanced connectivity in the rapidly evolving EV industry. For example, Wi-Fi continues to expand globally as the world's most affordable method of connecting the unconnected. Cisco forecasts the number of hotspots worldwide to reach 600 million this year. And as a market leader, Skyworks is uniquely positioned to benefit as deployments expand and the shift to Wi-Fi 7 drives increasing complexity. In addition, the average U.S. household today has more than 10 wirelessly connected devices. Each of these devices requires fast connections, low latency, and efficient battery life, all enabled by our integrated solutions. Further, the market for electric vehicles is expected to expand fourfold by 2027, leveraging our power isolation platforms, which are becoming a leading choice for global EV manufacturers. SkyWork's success in enabling these major technology transitions is underpinned by increasing demand for our leading-edge system solutions, differentiated by performance, integration, and most importantly, customer value. Moving forward, Skyworks is strategically equipped to capitalize on the rapidly changing connectivity landscape with an expanding set of customer relationships built over more than two decades, global scale and world-class manufacturing capabilities, a seasoned and talented workforce with a proven record of execution across multiple semiconductor cycles. and an efficient cash flow engine that funds innovation while providing consistent cash returns. With that, I will turn the call over to Chris for a discussion of last quarter's performance in our outlook for Q3.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Thanks, Liam. Skyworks revenue for the second fiscal quarter of 2023 was $1,153,000,000, exceeding consensus estimates. Mobile was approximately 60% of total revenue, with year-over-year revenue growth at our largest customer, reflecting broad content gains across their product portfolio. This revenue growth was offset by weakness in demand from the Android ecosystem, as it continues to destock inventory. Broad markets reached 40% of total revenue for the first time, with a strong contribution from the automotive, infrastructure, and industrial markets. Gross profit was $577 million, resulting in a gross margin of 50%. Operating expenses of $190 million declined on a sequential and year-over-year basis, given our focus on managing discretionary expense. We generated $386 million of operating income, translating into an operating margin of 33.5%. We incurred $13 million of other expense and our effective tax rate was 13.4%, driving net income of $323 million and diluted earnings per share of $2.02, in line with the guidance that we provided during the last earnings call. Now, turning to cash flow. Skyworks business model continues to deliver very strong cash generation. Second fiscal quarter cash flow from operations was 412 million, and capital expenditures were 45 million, resulting in a free cash flow of 366 million and cash flow margin of 32%. Through the first half of the fiscal year, we've generated record free cash flow of 1.1 billion and 43% free cash flow margin. Given our consistent level of profitability and lower CAPEX spending, we expect free cash flow margin to remain well above our target of 30% for the fiscal year. Also, during fiscal Q2, we paid $99 million in dividends, repurchased $9 million of scoured stock, and repaid $200 million of our variable rate term loan. In addition, we increased our cash and investment balance to almost $1.1 billion, to provide sufficient liquidity to repay 500 million of bonds that will reach maturity during fiscal Q3. Now let's move on to our outlook for Q3 of fiscal 2023. Taking into account the ongoing challenging macroeconomic environment and a slower than expected recovery and inventory destocking, especially in the Android ecosystem, we anticipate revenue for our third fiscal quarter between $1.5 billion and $1.9 billion. Gross margin is projected to be in the range of 47% to 48%, reflecting the cyclical impact of lower factory utilization while we are reducing our internal inventory levels. We expect operating expenses of approximately $183 to $187 million down sequentially and year over year as we are optimizing operating efficiencies. We will continue to make the necessary investments in technology and product development to further enhance our leadership position in mobile and drive diversification and growth in our broad markets business. Below the line, we anticipate roughly $13 million and other expense and an effective tax rate of 13.5% to 14%. We expect our diluted share count to be approximately 160 million shares. Accordingly, at the midpoint of the revenue range of $1.7 billion, we intend to deliver diluted earnings per share of $1.67. And with that, I'll turn the call back over to Liam.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Thanks, Chris. Skyworks has delivered solid results through the first half of our fiscal year, demonstrating strong profitability and record-free cash flow generation. With deep customer engagements underpinned by decades of technology investments and scale, Skyworks is well-equipped to lead and continue to outperform. Moving forward, the Skyworks team remains focused on driving operational efficiency while leveraging leading-edge technologies to capture opportunities across a dynamic market for connectivity. That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, let's open the line for questions.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin the question and answer session. Should you have a question, please press star followed by the one on your touchtone phone. You will hear a three-tone prompt acknowledging your request, and your questions will be pulled in the order they are received. Should you wish to decline from the pulling process, please press star 2. If you are using a speakerphone, please lift the handset before pressing any keys. Given time constraints, please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. One moment, please, for your first question. Your first question comes from Ambresh Srivastava with BMO. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk11
speakers.text: Hi, thank you very much. Excuse me, Chris and Liam, you guys have spoiled us. I have to go back, I don't know, 8, 10 years to see a four-handle on gross margin, and you have navigated through many quarters of sequential decline, going back 10 plus, 15, 20, and you're still being able to hold margin. So my first question is, What's going on in the margin front? Is it pricing? Is it something structurally different this time versus going back to the last eight, 10 years?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Yes, I'm British. I will take that question of you. And so, first of all, Q2, we delivered 50% gross margin, which was within our guidance range. But we started already seeing some of the underutilization charges hitting our income statement in the second quarter. For Q3, fiscal Q3, we guided 47 to 48%, as we are experiencing 400 to 500 basis points of underutilization charges, which are partially offset by ongoing cost reductions and operational efficiencies that we are driving. And the reason for the underutilization charges is a slower than expected recovery in the Android smartphone market, as they continue to work down inventory, their internal inventory, in a somewhat soft demand environment. Initially, we were anticipating a stronger second half of the fiscal year and calendar year, but we do see some signs of recovery, although I would say later and slower than initially anticipated. As a result of that, we are adjusting our factory utilizations across all our factories. That's resulting in those 400 to 500 basis points of underutilization charges. And I would like to note that, unfortunately, those underutilization charges are having a negative impact on the gross margin, but they do not have a negative impact on our cash flow. and we will continue to generate strong cash flow. And maybe last, we have been operating our business at a slightly elevated level of inventory in anticipation of a stronger recovery in the back half. Now that the recovery is going to be slower than expected, we are also going to adjust our internal inventory levels and right-size that Again, that doesn't help our gross margin, but it will further bolster our strong cash generation.

speakers.speaker: spk11
speakers.text: My follow-up is on the gross margin side. You're sitting at 185 days, and target level is 85, if I remember correctly, two years ago or three years ago you had given that to us. So if it has to come back to that level, then that headwind could sustain for more than a quarter. It could be a couple of quarters before inventory, at least two, three quarters before it normalizes. Am I thinking about it the right way?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Yeah, you think about it the right way. Well, first of all, inventory came slightly down already in Q2, but days were up on lower revenue. And so days will always be elevated in our two slowest seasonal quarters. and will improve in our stronger seasonal quarters. But we will bring down inventory and absolute dollars as well as in days of inventory on a normalized level. And that, of course, will, as a result of that, the gross margin will be on or about the same level for multiple quarters. And then eventually we'll As the business starts improving, margins will get back. And I get back to your first question, right? So this is not a pricing issue or this is not a major cost issue. It is just a temporarily underutilization issue.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Blaine Curtis with Barclays. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. Maybe I want to ask, you highlighted the weakness in Android. I think some other customers have seen some inventory correction in their largest customers. So I was curious what the percentage was in March and if you also have to work through some inventory at that customer.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: So the largest customer in March was approximately 64% of total revenue. And in terms of inventory, they manage their supply chain very well.

speakers.speaker: spk04
speakers.text: Okay. And then a perspective on the guide on broad markets, just kind of curious. It was down a little bit in March. How do you see that trending in June?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, Blaine, I mean, we definitely continue to diversify the broad markets portfolio. It continues to be, you know, very strategic for us. You know, we're capturing new design wins every month. Automotive has been strong. We've got a little bit more action going in Wi-Fi 7 and also in some of the infrastructure markets. So that business is looking really strong. And also the contribution from the INA portfolio continues to track well. So still a lot of bright spots there in the other side of the business. Obviously, Chris mentioned some of the unique headwinds in mobile, but there are also some really dynamic activities going on in the broad market space.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Vivek Ariya with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk10
speakers.text: Thanks for taking my question. I wanted to go back to where Skyworks is seeing the inventory issues because Liam and Chris, I remember you guys were very early and prudent to recognize the weakness in the China market last year. So I thought you had already taken care of the Android issue and any new issues would come with your largest customer. So I just wanted to reconfirm that the weakness you are seeing right now is still Android and not at your largest customer?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: So, in fact, that is correct. The weakness is that Android, and you are correct, we have proactively managed that as good as we can in terms of our component inventory in the channel. What we cannot control is the inventory level at the customer, at the phone level, and that's where the main culprit is, and we see our customers continue to destock in a soft demand environment.

speakers.speaker: spk10
speakers.text: All right. And follow up, you know, the fact that you are reducing factory utilization ahead of, you know, what is typically your strongest seasonal quarter, should we also be toning down our expectations of the, you know, mid-teens plus kind of sequential growth that you usually have in September, given all these macro factors?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: We only guide one quarter at a time here, but sitting here today, we do expect some good sequential growth in September and December. As you know, our largest customer ramps up their new product launches. As in the past, we will have some really good content in those phones that will ramp up in the back half of the calendar year.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Carl Ackerman with BNP Paribas. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk14
speakers.text: Yes, thank you. I guess, Chris, I wanted to just follow up on some of the inventory discussions earlier. Obviously, June tends to be the seasonally weakest period of the year for you, but But do you think you're actually shipping in line with sell-through at this point ahead of this seasonal ramp that you normally see in the second half of the year?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: So not in the Android ecosystem. We are still shipping below consumption because they still are burning through excess inventory at the phone level.

speakers.speaker: spk14
speakers.text: Got it. Got it. Okay. And then I guess, you know, just going back to the margin discussion earlier, When would you anticipate underutilization charges to abate? And I guess as you address that question, are there any risks to inventory obsolescence? If you could just discuss that as well, that'd be very helpful. Thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Right. So this is, as I said before, this is a multiple quarter event because it just takes time for those underutilization charges to actually hit the income statement, right? It goes through inventory turns until it hits your income statement. But we are seeing this soft demand environment in Android. It's improving, but slightly slower than expected. We are reducing inventory at the same time. And so this is a multi-quarter event. In terms of excess and obsolete, we don't see any major risk. We've managed pretty well through that.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, and just to jump in here, this is Liam. Obviously, you know, this is kind of a macro cycle that we're going through. I mean, every company has their own nuances here. But I would remind you, you know, the cash returns are very, very solid. You know, we paid our bills on CapEx. Free cash flow margins are going to be sustainable 30% plus. So there's a lot of positives around that. And, you know, we'll get through the cycle. We're very much focused on execution. And it has been a little tough from some of our customers. and so working with them and getting the inputs that drive our business. But we continue to drive design when penetration in new markets, whether they're in broad or even some of our mobile players and IoT players. So there's a lot of positives there. And, yeah, we're enduring a tough cycle, and I think we're doing the right things here to ensure a better future as we go forward. But the business is still quite solid. Cash returns are robust. We've got customer engagements that continue to ramp. And we're very confident on the outlook.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: The next question comes from Gary Mobley with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk05
speakers.text: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. I'd like to ask about your largest customer. In the first half of the fiscal year, you've managed to grow your business for them narrowly. So my question to you is, based on the content gains that you may see in the next generation platform from them, and all other things considered, do you think you can grow your revenue with them for the full year or, more importantly, second half this year versus last year?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, yeah. I mean, we can't give you the specifics, but we absolutely aspire to drive a better position in the second half on continuing to cement new programs that will get into 23 and 24.

speakers.speaker: spk11
speakers.text: Okay.

speakers.speaker: spk05
speakers.text: And on OpEx management, you're doing a good job at, I guess, tamping things down and, if not, decreasing your OpEx in this tough time. Does that involve any, I guess, proactive measures on headcount or MITED in the future?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Yeah, so we have been doing that. And you know Skyworks. We have been doing that consistently in the past. add headcount when needed in support of our technology and product roadmaps. And when things are getting tougher, we adjust. And we've made some downward adjustments in that area as well. Of course, making sure that we can continue to support our major customers, our major programs. And it's really focusing on driving operational efficiencies and trying to trim down some discretionary spending. That's what we focus on.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Edward Schneider with Chapter Equity Research. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk12
speakers.text: Thanks a lot. I'm a little confused, Lee. Maybe you could clear it up. Do you expect on a model model to see content up or down or flat in the second half of this year?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Ed, I missed the first part, Ed.

speakers.speaker: spk12
speakers.text: Sorry, I'm not looking for revenue guidance, because that's got all tangled up with macro and units and all that. I'm just looking at content in terms of new model releases year over year in the second half. Do you expect your content to be up, or should we expect it to be flatter down?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, we expect it to be up. That's our game plan. There's a lot of new technologies that emerge. and the leaders, and we're hanging around the hoop on every one of them. So, you know, we've got our teams working with the best customers and fielding the best opportunities. So we'll have to see how that plays out in the second half, but that's definitely where we're headed.

speakers.speaker: spk12
speakers.text: So in a fantasy world of flat units year over year, no change at all, you would naturally expect to be higher in revenue to your largest customer in the second half of the year, right?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: That would be our plan, yes.

speakers.speaker: spk12
speakers.text: Perfect. Okay. And then the Android, I know it's still kind of a mess. but there are some architectural changes going on at some of the flagship phones, even the low-end phones that are involved. I don't want to say integration, but more higher-density modules that will show up probably next year or so. I know Skyworks has kind of avoided some of that competition in the past just because there was ASP associated with it, but given that it kind of separates you from a lot of the domestic companies, suppliers in China, is it reasonable to assume that Skyworks would participate more aggressively in the Android food chain, say, in 5G smartphone with their entry or flagship in the next two years?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, Ed, I would say yes to that because now as those models in Asia and Android become more complex, that's right up our alley, right? I mean, so our aperture is more to the mid to the high end, and we want to lift those customers and help them create a better engine and a better solution. So we're there. And there's a lot of upside for us and that characteristic because we've been a little bit more high in play. But as the complexity gets more and more embedded, that creates more and more opportunities for us. It's hard to hit the hard pitch, right? We know how to do that. But we also got to take care of the other business as well. So we feel good about it. We definitely have... to know how to make it work. And I think it will be part of the recovery here as we get through the middle of the year.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Harsh Kumar with Piper Sandler. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Yeah, hey, guys. I was curious, Liam, if you could give us a sense of how much excess inventory of complete hand sets is in the Chinese on market. In other words, I guess what I'm trying to understand is I know you're under shipping, curious how long or how many quarters it might take for sell-in to equal to sell-out.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Right. Half. We don't have a specific number on the number of access inventory on the handset level, but it is a couple quarters, right? And initially we anticipated it to be a couple quarters, but now It might be a couple quarters more, and that's the feedback we are getting from the customers. That's the feedback and remarks that we see by our peers and competitors.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: That's fair, guys. And then for my follow-up, if I can ask you if you could help us out with broadband. Do you think that broadband might be up in the June quarter on a sequential basis or year-over-year basis? Any color would be great.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Right, so our broke markets business will be slightly down on a sequential basis into the June quarter. Again, as Liam already talked about that, right, we see certain areas of strength in automotive, some of our industrial markets, but... There is some inventory overhang in some of the more consumer enterprise-oriented markets. Again, very similar to what has been mentioned by peers and competitors that play in this field.

speakers.speaker: spk08
speakers.text: Fair enough, guys. Thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Ruben Roy with Stiefel. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk02
speakers.text: Thank you. Thanks for letting me ask the question. Harsh asked the essence of my question, Liam, but I guess specifically on auto, was it up in the March quarter, and do you expect auto to continue to remain strong as you sort of characterized? And the reason I'm asking that is, you know, obviously there were some long lead times and that type of thing in auto components. I'm wondering, you know, how lead times look. Are they coming in and what the inventory assessment is in that market specifically as you think about the rest of the year? Thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, sure. Great question. As you know, we actually hadn't done much in automotive two, three years ago, and we're now really making great progress. So the good news there, there's a tremendous amount of new territory that we can cover in automotive. We've already won a number of platforms and programs with key OEMs, EV players, et cetera. The partnership with our INA business has been a real catalyst there as well for us. So it's a fast-growing part of our portfolio. It has tremendous upside. We have low share relative to the pie, and that's going to make for pretty dynamic opportunities as we go forward. It's definitely a grower for us this year. Despite all this inventory stuff we talked about, the auto market will definitely grow.

speakers.speaker: spk02
speakers.text: That's helpful. Thanks, Liam. And just a quick follow-up on Ed's question earlier, and sort of thinking through design activity for next year maybe in Android, how would you characterize that? It seems like there are a lot of insurgents moving to single module right now. Would you characterize design activity as strong right now, ahead of sort of those ramps, or do you think that's still something on the come that you guys will be participating in bake-offs in later this year? What's the timing on that, I guess, is the question.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, well, I mean, as you know, we've been focusing more, you know, high-end, mid-tier, et cetera, but obviously now the good news is that our customers want better performance. So, you know, we had been a little bit more cautious in engaging in some of the lower-end markets, but some of those products now and the appetite for connectivity is raised, which makes it much more profitable and more in the, you know, kind of down the alley for Skyworks. So you're going to see more opportunities for us uh emerge in in in the android cycle uh you know samsung's doing a lot better google's a player now for us we're doing a lot there uh and obviously you know the players in china china's been a little tough but i think that that will come back and that will be another catalyst for so we know how to make all that stuff and that stuff is is is not new at all we know exactly how to handle it uh automotive again is a new market that we're doing very well on and i think you know, we get through some of these macro headwinds, we'll be able to really kind of shine a light on some of these strategic design wins that we have.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Harlan Sir with JP Morgan. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk15
speakers.text: Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. On broad markets, I think 90 days ago, you guys had anticipated driving four-year growth in this segment. But as you just mentioned, you know, you've got dynamics in the consumer IOT market. I think even data center enterprise telco markets have continued to soften a bit here. So does the team still believe that they can drive full-year growth in broad markets?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Yeah, I think, Harlan, I think that's going to be a challenge, right? So what we said is that we were expect them some modest year-over-year growth on a calendar year basis. But given some of the macroeconomic challenges that we have seen with high inflation and increased interest rates and the impact it has on consumer and enterprise spending, I think this is going to be challenging. Having said that, I mean, now I'm looking beyond calendar year 23 into fiscal 24, we do expect our growth markets business to grow in fiscal 24 over fiscal 23.

speakers.speaker: spk15
speakers.text: Perfect. And then, you know, the team has done a great job, you know, proliferating your filter technology. I think last year, I think the team drove about 45% ball filter attached to your mobile revenues, right? Given the design wind pipeline for this year, on new model launches in the second half. Where do you see that attach rate moving to?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Yeah, that attach rate continues to move higher and higher, and there's multiple nodes and bulk acoustic waves. So it's not one that fits all. There's a lot of innovation. There's a tremendous amount of R&D. And one of the other things that we talked about a little bit is our capital intensity. That's a plus for us as well. We've already gone through a pretty significant cycle in raising the capability and technology nodes with VAW. We have a lot of capacity right now that we're ready to roll on. And it's a strategic technology. Not many companies know how to do it. And it can go beyond the smartphone as well. So the applications certainly today are in handsets, but there's a broader set of opportunities where VAW filter is a meaningful part of the strategy and meaningful part of the performance. So you'll be able to see that more as we go through this year and following years.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your next question comes from Kevin Cassidy with Rosenblatt Securities. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Yes, thanks for taking my question. And I just want to understand, too, as you cut back on utilization, what's the shape of being able to bring that back up again? I guess if it Do your lead times start to stretch out, and that's when you build your utilization back up again? Just kind of what's the strategy as business starts to come back?

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Yeah, so a lot of it will depend on how strong the business will bounce back. And once we start seeing it, we already see it, right? Some of recovery in the Android market, once that gets stronger, In combination then, of course, with continuing to grow our broad markets business, as we just indicated, and doing well with our largest customer, we will start ramping up the factory utilizations. But as I said earlier, it's a couple of quarters, and then that will bounce back.

speakers.speaker: spk13
speakers.text: Okay, but to bring utilization back up, it's just a matter of rehiring people? It doesn't mean new equipment? You've just turned the equipment off?

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: No, the equipment's there. I mean, we basically know how to handle that. You know, the capital, the scale, all that's ready to go. This is just more of a demand issue, but we know how to handle it. And there's going to be a tremendous amount of activity that will go through those cycles and go through those factories, leveraging that capital, which is in great position and has – tremendous opportunity over the next several years to populate not only smartphones, as we said, but other bulk acoustic wave type of engines.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Your last question comes from Matt Ramsey with TD Cowan. Please go ahead.

speakers.speaker: spk03
speakers.text: Thank you very much, guys. Good afternoon. I guess my first question, some of your peer companies that also have Some pretty high revenue exposure to your largest customer talked about a dynamic of maybe them buying a bit more early in this calendar year, pulling in some of their own inventory purchases and leaving a bit of air pocket before things ramp in the backup. Are you guys, is some of the stuff reflected in the guidance that type of dynamic? Or is it more lean toward Android, as you've mentioned in some of your prepared comments? Thanks. yeah it's more towards the android side at that point the way we go here and so i think that that's maybe what you're seeing but but uh and there again i mean we know how to manage through it got it um i guess i guess chris i wanted to ask a longer term thing as my follow-up um and it's on free cash flow um you you mentioned that some of the utilization charge things that are going to happen in the short term with the factories are not cash flow hits uh but Given the dynamics in the business, could you talk a little bit about how – are there any specific floors of free cash flow that you're managing to in terms of a free cash flow percentage? And just how do you think you plan to manage the business over the next two, three years on a cash flow basis? I think that would be helpful. Thanks.

speakers.speaker: spk09
speakers.text: Yeah, that's a great question. And so our target model is a free cash flow margin of 30%. In the last couple of years, we have been operating the business in the mid to high 20s. And the reason why we were not at 30% is, as Liam just explained, we have made major investments in our technology, in our manufacturing assets, building out very high-class technology. manufacturing capabilities. But looking forward over the next couple years, instead of running CapEx at 10 or 12% to revenue, we believe that in the next couple years we can run the business at mid-single digits as a percent to revenue for CapEx. In addition to that, of course, we will continue to grow the business and run the business at high profit levels And when you combine that with good working capital management, we believe we will be able to sustainably run this business at 30, 30 plus percent free cash flow margin. And again, just in the first six months of the year here, we've already generated more cash than we did last year, right? With $1.1 billion of free cash flow at 43% free cash flow margin. But again, sustainably well above 30%. for the remainder of or the total of the fiscal year.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: There are no further questions at this time. Please proceed.

speakers.speaker: spk06
speakers.text: Thanks for participating in today's call. We look forward to talking to you at upcoming investor conferences during the quarter. Thank you.

speakers.speaker: spk01
speakers.text: Ladies and gentlemen, this concludes your conference call for today. We thank you for participating and ask that you please disconnect your lines.

spk06.name: Liam Griffin
spk06.title: Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President

text:
Joelle (Conference Operator): Good afternoon and welcome to the Skyworks Solutions second quarter fiscal year 2023 earnings call. This call is being recorded. At this time, I will turn the call over to Mitch Hayes, investor relations for Skyworks. Mr. Hayes, please go ahead.

Mitch Hayes (Investor Relations): Thank you, Joelle. Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Skyworks second fiscal quarter 2023 conference call. With me today are Liam Griffin, our chairman, chief executive officer and president, and Chris Senesal, our Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, I would like to remind everyone that our discussion will include statements relating to future results and expectations that are or may be considered forward-looking statements. Please refer to our earnings press release and recent SEC filings, including our annual report on Form 10-K, for information on certain risks that could cause actual outcomes to differ materially and adversely from any forward-looking statements made today. The results and guidance we will discuss include non-GAAP financial measures consistent with our past practice. Please refer to our press release within the investor relations section of our company website for complete reconciliation to GAAP. With that, I'll turn the call to Liam.

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Thanks, Mitch, and welcome, everyone. The Skyworks team executed well in a challenging market environment, delivering second quarter revenue above consensus estimates with solid profitability and strong cash flow generation. Looking at Q2 in more detail, we delivered revenue of $1,153,000,000. We drove gross margin of 50% and operating margin of 33.5%. We posted earnings per share of $2.02 and we generated $412,000,000 of operating cash flow. In addition to the financial results, we expanded our design wind pipeline reflecting our success in diversifying our customer base and product portfolio. Across mobile and IoT, we delivered Sky5 platforms for Samsung's newly released smartphones. We launched Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 gateways for CommScope and Asus. And we secured 5G content with a mobile computing leader. Across infrastructure and industrial, we enable small cell deployments with a Japanese telecommunications company. We provided enhanced power over ethernet functionality to Cisco for their enterprise networks. We shipped programmable timing solutions to the top US satellite provider and leveraged our expanding industrial product suite with a leader in smart meter technology. In automotive, we continue to post year-over-year revenue growth while capturing EV onboard charging content with a top European supplier and ramping digital radio products with a leading Korean OEM. These engagements highlight the increasingly diverse and expansive nature of our business, supporting the broadest array of customers and applications in our history. Several key market trends underscore the growth potential of advanced connectivity in the rapidly evolving EV industry. For example, Wi-Fi continues to expand globally as the world's most affordable method of connecting the unconnected. Cisco forecasts the number of hotspots worldwide to reach 600 million this year. And as a market leader, Skyworks is uniquely positioned to benefit as deployments expand and the shift to Wi-Fi 7 drives increasing complexity. In addition, the average U.S. household today has more than 10 wirelessly connected devices. Each of these devices requires fast connections, low latency, and efficient battery life, all enabled by our integrated solutions. Further, the market for electric vehicles is expected to expand fourfold by 2027, leveraging our power isolation platforms, which are becoming a leading choice for global EV manufacturers. SkyWork's success in enabling these major technology transitions is underpinned by increasing demand for our leading-edge system solutions, differentiated by performance, integration, and most importantly, customer value. Moving forward, Skyworks is strategically equipped to capitalize on the rapidly changing connectivity landscape with an expanding set of customer relationships built over more than two decades, global scale and world-class manufacturing capabilities, a seasoned and talented workforce with a proven record of execution across multiple semiconductor cycles. and an efficient cash flow engine that funds innovation while providing consistent cash returns. With that, I will turn the call over to Chris for a discussion of last quarter's performance in our outlook for Q3.

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Thanks, Liam. Skyworks revenue for the second fiscal quarter of 2023 was $1,153,000,000, exceeding consensus estimates. Mobile was approximately 60% of total revenue, with year-over-year revenue growth at our largest customer, reflecting broad content gains across their product portfolio. This revenue growth was offset by weakness in demand from the Android ecosystem, as it continues to destock inventory. Broad markets reached 40% of total revenue for the first time, with a strong contribution from the automotive, infrastructure, and industrial markets. Gross profit was $577 million, resulting in a gross margin of 50%. Operating expenses of $190 million declined on a sequential and year-over-year basis, given our focus on managing discretionary expense. We generated $386 million of operating income, translating into an operating margin of 33.5%. We incurred $13 million of other expense and our effective tax rate was 13.4%, driving net income of $323 million and diluted earnings per share of $2.02, in line with the guidance that we provided during the last earnings call. Now, turning to cash flow. Skyworks business model continues to deliver very strong cash generation. Second fiscal quarter cash flow from operations was 412 million, and capital expenditures were 45 million, resulting in a free cash flow of 366 million and cash flow margin of 32%. Through the first half of the fiscal year, we've generated record free cash flow of 1.1 billion and 43% free cash flow margin. Given our consistent level of profitability and lower CAPEX spending, we expect free cash flow margin to remain well above our target of 30% for the fiscal year. Also, during fiscal Q2, we paid $99 million in dividends, repurchased $9 million of scoured stock, and repaid $200 million of our variable rate term loan. In addition, we increased our cash and investment balance to almost $1.1 billion, to provide sufficient liquidity to repay 500 million of bonds that will reach maturity during fiscal Q3. Now let's move on to our outlook for Q3 of fiscal 2023. Taking into account the ongoing challenging macroeconomic environment and a slower than expected recovery and inventory destocking, especially in the Android ecosystem, we anticipate revenue for our third fiscal quarter between $1.5 billion and $1.9 billion. Gross margin is projected to be in the range of 47% to 48%, reflecting the cyclical impact of lower factory utilization while we are reducing our internal inventory levels. We expect operating expenses of approximately $183 to $187 million down sequentially and year over year as we are optimizing operating efficiencies. We will continue to make the necessary investments in technology and product development to further enhance our leadership position in mobile and drive diversification and growth in our broad markets business. Below the line, we anticipate roughly $13 million and other expense and an effective tax rate of 13.5% to 14%. We expect our diluted share count to be approximately 160 million shares. Accordingly, at the midpoint of the revenue range of $1.7 billion, we intend to deliver diluted earnings per share of $1.67. And with that, I'll turn the call back over to Liam.

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Thanks, Chris. Skyworks has delivered solid results through the first half of our fiscal year, demonstrating strong profitability and record-free cash flow generation. With deep customer engagements underpinned by decades of technology investments and scale, Skyworks is well-equipped to lead and continue to outperform. Moving forward, the Skyworks team remains focused on driving operational efficiency while leveraging leading-edge technologies to capture opportunities across a dynamic market for connectivity. That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, let's open the line for questions.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin the question and answer session. Should you have a question, please press star followed by the one on your touchtone phone. You will hear a three-tone prompt acknowledging your request, and your questions will be pulled in the order they are received. Should you wish to decline from the pulling process, please press star 2. If you are using a speakerphone, please lift the handset before pressing any keys. Given time constraints, please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. One moment, please, for your first question. Your first question comes from Ambresh Srivastava with BMO. Please go ahead.

Ambresh Srivastava (Analyst at BMO Capital Markets): Hi, thank you very much. Excuse me, Chris and Liam, you guys have spoiled us. I have to go back, I don't know, 8, 10 years to see a four-handle on gross margin, and you have navigated through many quarters of sequential decline, going back 10 plus, 15, 20, and you're still being able to hold margin. So my first question is, What's going on in the margin front? Is it pricing? Is it something structurally different this time versus going back to the last eight, 10 years?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Yes, I'm British. I will take that question of you. And so, first of all, Q2, we delivered 50% gross margin, which was within our guidance range. But we started already seeing some of the underutilization charges hitting our income statement in the second quarter. For Q3, fiscal Q3, we guided 47 to 48%, as we are experiencing 400 to 500 basis points of underutilization charges, which are partially offset by ongoing cost reductions and operational efficiencies that we are driving. And the reason for the underutilization charges is a slower than expected recovery in the Android smartphone market, as they continue to work down inventory, their internal inventory, in a somewhat soft demand environment. Initially, we were anticipating a stronger second half of the fiscal year and calendar year, but we do see some signs of recovery, although I would say later and slower than initially anticipated. As a result of that, we are adjusting our factory utilizations across all our factories. That's resulting in those 400 to 500 basis points of underutilization charges. And I would like to note that, unfortunately, those underutilization charges are having a negative impact on the gross margin, but they do not have a negative impact on our cash flow. and we will continue to generate strong cash flow. And maybe last, we have been operating our business at a slightly elevated level of inventory in anticipation of a stronger recovery in the back half. Now that the recovery is going to be slower than expected, we are also going to adjust our internal inventory levels and right-size that Again, that doesn't help our gross margin, but it will further bolster our strong cash generation.

Ambresh Srivastava (Analyst at BMO Capital Markets): My follow-up is on the gross margin side. You're sitting at 185 days, and target level is 85, if I remember correctly, two years ago or three years ago you had given that to us. So if it has to come back to that level, then that headwind could sustain for more than a quarter. It could be a couple of quarters before inventory, at least two, three quarters before it normalizes. Am I thinking about it the right way?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Yeah, you think about it the right way. Well, first of all, inventory came slightly down already in Q2, but days were up on lower revenue. And so days will always be elevated in our two slowest seasonal quarters. and will improve in our stronger seasonal quarters. But we will bring down inventory and absolute dollars as well as in days of inventory on a normalized level. And that, of course, will, as a result of that, the gross margin will be on or about the same level for multiple quarters. And then eventually we'll As the business starts improving, margins will get back. And I get back to your first question, right? So this is not a pricing issue or this is not a major cost issue. It is just a temporarily underutilization issue.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Blaine Curtis with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Blaine Curtis (Analyst at Barclays): Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. Maybe I want to ask, you highlighted the weakness in Android. I think some other customers have seen some inventory correction in their largest customers. So I was curious what the percentage was in March and if you also have to work through some inventory at that customer.

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): So the largest customer in March was approximately 64% of total revenue. And in terms of inventory, they manage their supply chain very well.

Blaine Curtis (Analyst at Barclays): Okay. And then a perspective on the guide on broad markets, just kind of curious. It was down a little bit in March. How do you see that trending in June?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, Blaine, I mean, we definitely continue to diversify the broad markets portfolio. It continues to be, you know, very strategic for us. You know, we're capturing new design wins every month. Automotive has been strong. We've got a little bit more action going in Wi-Fi 7 and also in some of the infrastructure markets. So that business is looking really strong. And also the contribution from the INA portfolio continues to track well. So still a lot of bright spots there in the other side of the business. Obviously, Chris mentioned some of the unique headwinds in mobile, but there are also some really dynamic activities going on in the broad market space.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Vivek Ariya with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Vivek Ariya (Analyst at Bank of America): Thanks for taking my question. I wanted to go back to where Skyworks is seeing the inventory issues because Liam and Chris, I remember you guys were very early and prudent to recognize the weakness in the China market last year. So I thought you had already taken care of the Android issue and any new issues would come with your largest customer. So I just wanted to reconfirm that the weakness you are seeing right now is still Android and not at your largest customer?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): So, in fact, that is correct. The weakness is that Android, and you are correct, we have proactively managed that as good as we can in terms of our component inventory in the channel. What we cannot control is the inventory level at the customer, at the phone level, and that's where the main culprit is, and we see our customers continue to destock in a soft demand environment.

Vivek Ariya (Analyst at Bank of America): All right. And follow up, you know, the fact that you are reducing factory utilization ahead of, you know, what is typically your strongest seasonal quarter, should we also be toning down our expectations of the, you know, mid-teens plus kind of sequential growth that you usually have in September, given all these macro factors?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): We only guide one quarter at a time here, but sitting here today, we do expect some good sequential growth in September and December. As you know, our largest customer ramps up their new product launches. As in the past, we will have some really good content in those phones that will ramp up in the back half of the calendar year.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Carl Ackerman with BNP Paribas. Please go ahead.

Carl Ackerman (Analyst at BNP Paribas): Yes, thank you. I guess, Chris, I wanted to just follow up on some of the inventory discussions earlier. Obviously, June tends to be the seasonally weakest period of the year for you, but But do you think you're actually shipping in line with sell-through at this point ahead of this seasonal ramp that you normally see in the second half of the year?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): So not in the Android ecosystem. We are still shipping below consumption because they still are burning through excess inventory at the phone level.

Carl Ackerman (Analyst at BNP Paribas): Got it. Got it. Okay. And then I guess, you know, just going back to the margin discussion earlier, When would you anticipate underutilization charges to abate? And I guess as you address that question, are there any risks to inventory obsolescence? If you could just discuss that as well, that'd be very helpful. Thank you.

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Right. So this is, as I said before, this is a multiple quarter event because it just takes time for those underutilization charges to actually hit the income statement, right? It goes through inventory turns until it hits your income statement. But we are seeing this soft demand environment in Android. It's improving, but slightly slower than expected. We are reducing inventory at the same time. And so this is a multi-quarter event. In terms of excess and obsolete, we don't see any major risk. We've managed pretty well through that.

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, and just to jump in here, this is Liam. Obviously, you know, this is kind of a macro cycle that we're going through. I mean, every company has their own nuances here. But I would remind you, you know, the cash returns are very, very solid. You know, we paid our bills on CapEx. Free cash flow margins are going to be sustainable 30% plus. So there's a lot of positives around that. And, you know, we'll get through the cycle. We're very much focused on execution. And it has been a little tough from some of our customers. and so working with them and getting the inputs that drive our business. But we continue to drive design when penetration in new markets, whether they're in broad or even some of our mobile players and IoT players. So there's a lot of positives there. And, yeah, we're enduring a tough cycle, and I think we're doing the right things here to ensure a better future as we go forward. But the business is still quite solid. Cash returns are robust. We've got customer engagements that continue to ramp. And we're very confident on the outlook.

Joelle (Conference Operator): The next question comes from Gary Mobley with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

Gary Mobley (Analyst at Wells Fargo): Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. I'd like to ask about your largest customer. In the first half of the fiscal year, you've managed to grow your business for them narrowly. So my question to you is, based on the content gains that you may see in the next generation platform from them, and all other things considered, do you think you can grow your revenue with them for the full year or, more importantly, second half this year versus last year?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, yeah. I mean, we can't give you the specifics, but we absolutely aspire to drive a better position in the second half on continuing to cement new programs that will get into 23 and 24.

Ambresh Srivastava (Analyst at BMO Capital Markets): Okay.

Gary Mobley (Analyst at Wells Fargo): And on OpEx management, you're doing a good job at, I guess, tamping things down and, if not, decreasing your OpEx in this tough time. Does that involve any, I guess, proactive measures on headcount or MITED in the future?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Yeah, so we have been doing that. And you know Skyworks. We have been doing that consistently in the past. add headcount when needed in support of our technology and product roadmaps. And when things are getting tougher, we adjust. And we've made some downward adjustments in that area as well. Of course, making sure that we can continue to support our major customers, our major programs. And it's really focusing on driving operational efficiencies and trying to trim down some discretionary spending. That's what we focus on.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Edward Schneider with Chapter Equity Research. Please go ahead.

Edward Schneider (Analyst at Chapter Equity Research): Thanks a lot. I'm a little confused, Lee. Maybe you could clear it up. Do you expect on a model model to see content up or down or flat in the second half of this year?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Ed, I missed the first part, Ed.

Edward Schneider (Analyst at Chapter Equity Research): Sorry, I'm not looking for revenue guidance, because that's got all tangled up with macro and units and all that. I'm just looking at content in terms of new model releases year over year in the second half. Do you expect your content to be up, or should we expect it to be flatter down?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, we expect it to be up. That's our game plan. There's a lot of new technologies that emerge. and the leaders, and we're hanging around the hoop on every one of them. So, you know, we've got our teams working with the best customers and fielding the best opportunities. So we'll have to see how that plays out in the second half, but that's definitely where we're headed.

Edward Schneider (Analyst at Chapter Equity Research): So in a fantasy world of flat units year over year, no change at all, you would naturally expect to be higher in revenue to your largest customer in the second half of the year, right?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): That would be our plan, yes.

Edward Schneider (Analyst at Chapter Equity Research): Perfect. Okay. And then the Android, I know it's still kind of a mess. but there are some architectural changes going on at some of the flagship phones, even the low-end phones that are involved. I don't want to say integration, but more higher-density modules that will show up probably next year or so. I know Skyworks has kind of avoided some of that competition in the past just because there was ASP associated with it, but given that it kind of separates you from a lot of the domestic companies, suppliers in China, is it reasonable to assume that Skyworks would participate more aggressively in the Android food chain, say, in 5G smartphone with their entry or flagship in the next two years?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, Ed, I would say yes to that because now as those models in Asia and Android become more complex, that's right up our alley, right? I mean, so our aperture is more to the mid to the high end, and we want to lift those customers and help them create a better engine and a better solution. So we're there. And there's a lot of upside for us and that characteristic because we've been a little bit more high in play. But as the complexity gets more and more embedded, that creates more and more opportunities for us. It's hard to hit the hard pitch, right? We know how to do that. But we also got to take care of the other business as well. So we feel good about it. We definitely have... to know how to make it work. And I think it will be part of the recovery here as we get through the middle of the year.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Harsh Kumar with Piper Sandler. Please go ahead.

Harsh Kumar (Analyst at Piper Sandler): Yeah, hey, guys. I was curious, Liam, if you could give us a sense of how much excess inventory of complete hand sets is in the Chinese on market. In other words, I guess what I'm trying to understand is I know you're under shipping, curious how long or how many quarters it might take for sell-in to equal to sell-out.

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Right. Half. We don't have a specific number on the number of access inventory on the handset level, but it is a couple quarters, right? And initially we anticipated it to be a couple quarters, but now It might be a couple quarters more, and that's the feedback we are getting from the customers. That's the feedback and remarks that we see by our peers and competitors.

Harsh Kumar (Analyst at Piper Sandler): That's fair, guys. And then for my follow-up, if I can ask you if you could help us out with broadband. Do you think that broadband might be up in the June quarter on a sequential basis or year-over-year basis? Any color would be great.

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Right, so our broke markets business will be slightly down on a sequential basis into the June quarter. Again, as Liam already talked about that, right, we see certain areas of strength in automotive, some of our industrial markets, but... There is some inventory overhang in some of the more consumer enterprise-oriented markets. Again, very similar to what has been mentioned by peers and competitors that play in this field.

Harsh Kumar (Analyst at Piper Sandler): Fair enough, guys. Thank you.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Ruben Roy with Stiefel. Please go ahead.

Ruben Roy (Analyst at Stifel): Thank you. Thanks for letting me ask the question. Harsh asked the essence of my question, Liam, but I guess specifically on auto, was it up in the March quarter, and do you expect auto to continue to remain strong as you sort of characterized? And the reason I'm asking that is, you know, obviously there were some long lead times and that type of thing in auto components. I'm wondering, you know, how lead times look. Are they coming in and what the inventory assessment is in that market specifically as you think about the rest of the year? Thank you.

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, sure. Great question. As you know, we actually hadn't done much in automotive two, three years ago, and we're now really making great progress. So the good news there, there's a tremendous amount of new territory that we can cover in automotive. We've already won a number of platforms and programs with key OEMs, EV players, et cetera. The partnership with our INA business has been a real catalyst there as well for us. So it's a fast-growing part of our portfolio. It has tremendous upside. We have low share relative to the pie, and that's going to make for pretty dynamic opportunities as we go forward. It's definitely a grower for us this year. Despite all this inventory stuff we talked about, the auto market will definitely grow.

Ruben Roy (Analyst at Stifel): That's helpful. Thanks, Liam. And just a quick follow-up on Ed's question earlier, and sort of thinking through design activity for next year maybe in Android, how would you characterize that? It seems like there are a lot of insurgents moving to single module right now. Would you characterize design activity as strong right now, ahead of sort of those ramps, or do you think that's still something on the come that you guys will be participating in bake-offs in later this year? What's the timing on that, I guess, is the question.

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, well, I mean, as you know, we've been focusing more, you know, high-end, mid-tier, et cetera, but obviously now the good news is that our customers want better performance. So, you know, we had been a little bit more cautious in engaging in some of the lower-end markets, but some of those products now and the appetite for connectivity is raised, which makes it much more profitable and more in the, you know, kind of down the alley for Skyworks. So you're going to see more opportunities for us uh emerge in in in the android cycle uh you know samsung's doing a lot better google's a player now for us we're doing a lot there uh and obviously you know the players in china china's been a little tough but i think that that will come back and that will be another catalyst for so we know how to make all that stuff and that stuff is is is not new at all we know exactly how to handle it uh automotive again is a new market that we're doing very well on and i think you know, we get through some of these macro headwinds, we'll be able to really kind of shine a light on some of these strategic design wins that we have.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Harlan Sir with JP Morgan. Please go ahead.

Harlan Sir (Analyst at J.P. Morgan): Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. On broad markets, I think 90 days ago, you guys had anticipated driving four-year growth in this segment. But as you just mentioned, you know, you've got dynamics in the consumer IOT market. I think even data center enterprise telco markets have continued to soften a bit here. So does the team still believe that they can drive full-year growth in broad markets?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Yeah, I think, Harlan, I think that's going to be a challenge, right? So what we said is that we were expect them some modest year-over-year growth on a calendar year basis. But given some of the macroeconomic challenges that we have seen with high inflation and increased interest rates and the impact it has on consumer and enterprise spending, I think this is going to be challenging. Having said that, I mean, now I'm looking beyond calendar year 23 into fiscal 24, we do expect our growth markets business to grow in fiscal 24 over fiscal 23.

Harlan Sir (Analyst at J.P. Morgan): Perfect. And then, you know, the team has done a great job, you know, proliferating your filter technology. I think last year, I think the team drove about 45% ball filter attached to your mobile revenues, right? Given the design wind pipeline for this year, on new model launches in the second half. Where do you see that attach rate moving to?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): Yeah, that attach rate continues to move higher and higher, and there's multiple nodes and bulk acoustic waves. So it's not one that fits all. There's a lot of innovation. There's a tremendous amount of R&D. And one of the other things that we talked about a little bit is our capital intensity. That's a plus for us as well. We've already gone through a pretty significant cycle in raising the capability and technology nodes with VAW. We have a lot of capacity right now that we're ready to roll on. And it's a strategic technology. Not many companies know how to do it. And it can go beyond the smartphone as well. So the applications certainly today are in handsets, but there's a broader set of opportunities where VAW filter is a meaningful part of the strategy and meaningful part of the performance. So you'll be able to see that more as we go through this year and following years.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your next question comes from Kevin Cassidy with Rosenblatt Securities. Please go ahead.

Kevin Cassidy (Analyst at Rosenblatt Securities): Yes, thanks for taking my question. And I just want to understand, too, as you cut back on utilization, what's the shape of being able to bring that back up again? I guess if it Do your lead times start to stretch out, and that's when you build your utilization back up again? Just kind of what's the strategy as business starts to come back?

Chris Senesal (Chief Financial Officer): Yeah, so a lot of it will depend on how strong the business will bounce back. And once we start seeing it, we already see it, right? Some of recovery in the Android market, once that gets stronger, In combination then, of course, with continuing to grow our broad markets business, as we just indicated, and doing well with our largest customer, we will start ramping up the factory utilizations. But as I said earlier, it's a couple of quarters, and then that will bounce back.

Kevin Cassidy (Analyst at Rosenblatt Securities): Okay, but to bring utilization back up, it's just a matter of rehiring people? It doesn't mean new equipment? You've just turned the equipment off?

Liam Griffin (Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and President): No, the equipment's there. I mean, we basically know how to handle that. You know, the capital, the scale, all that's ready to go. This is just more of a demand issue, but we know how to handle it. And there's going to be a tremendous amount of activity that will go through those cycles and go through those factories, leveraging that capital, which is in great position and has – tremendous opportunity over the next several years to populate not only smartphones, as we said, but other bulk acoustic wave type of engines.

Joelle (Conference Operator): Your last question comes from Matt Ramsey with TD Cowan. Please go ahead.

Matt Ramsey (Analyst at TD Cowen): Thank you very much, guys. Good afternoon.
